hero.kicker: Fall cleanup and leaf removal in Grand Blanc, MI
hero.title: Leaves up. **Lawn back.**
hero.lede: Grand Scapes blows the leaves off the lawn and out of the beds, vacuums them into our leaf trailer and hauls them away. Then the beds get cut back the way you want them and the drive and walks are blown clean. We do fall cleanups all over Grand Blanc and Genesee County.

blocks.title: Blow, vacuum, **haul.**
body: Fall cleanup is leaf removal plus the end of season tidy. The crew blows the leaves off the lawn, out of the beds and away from the fences into long rows and piles. A truck loader leaf vacuum on the front of our dump trailer pulls them in, and the load leaves with us.
No bags lined up at the curb and no raking weekends. Once the leaves are gone, we cut back the beds you want cut back and blow off the drive, the walks and the patio.

We do fall cleanups across Grand Blanc and Grand Blanc Township, and around Genesee County in towns like [Fenton](/leaf-removal-fenton-mi/), [Flint](/leaf-removal-flint-mi/), [Davison](/leaf-removal-davison-mi/) and [Holly](/leaf-removal-holly-mi/).

blocks.title: Drag the leaves **off the lawn.**
blocks.intro: An illustration of a yard the week after the big drop. Drag across it to clear the lawn and the beds, the way a cleanup does.

blocks.title: Mulch a few, **move a lot.**
blocks.intro: Michigan State University Extension research is clear that a light layer of leaves can be mowed right into a lawn. The trouble is a thick layer left to sit through the winter.

items.title: Mow it in
items.body: In MSU studies, up to 6 inches of leaves were mowed into lawns with no harm, and the bits sifted into the grass within a few weeks. For a light drop, a mower with a sharp blade is all it takes.

items.title: Get it off
items.body: MSU's mulching advice is not to let leaves get deeper than 3 to 4 inches before mowing them in. Left in a thick layer under wet, heavy snow, MSU says, leaves can mean disaster for the grass below.

items.title: When the drop wins
items.body: Under big, old trees the leaves can come down faster than a mower keeps up with. MSU notes that after heavy wind, even mulching them in can take two passes in a week. That is the yard the leaf vacuum is for.

items.title: Your call
items.body: MSU suggests leaves can stay around shrubs and perennials over winter as insulation and shelter for insects, with some stems left standing for bees. Some people want the beds cleared to the soil instead. Tell Rob which.

blocks.title: The last mow, **one notch down.**
body: The final mow of the year comes once the grass stops growing, not on a set date. MSU Extension suggests lowering the mower no more than one notch, about half an inch, for that cut. It picks up the last leaf bits and keeps the grass from going into winter too tall, which MSU says reduces trouble with voles and snow mold.

On lawns we already mow every week, that last cut is simply the end of the season. For everyone else, we can bag a final cut once the leaves are out, so the lawn goes into winter clean and striped one more time.

blocks.title: Our own **fall photos.**

blocks.title: Leaves now, **plow next.**
blocks.intro: Fall cleanup sits between the last mow and the first snow. Lay out the whole year, from spring cleanup and weekly mowing to a plowed drive in winter, and Rob can quote it together.

faq.q: Do you do leaf removal in Grand Blanc?
faq.a: Yes. Grand Scapes does fall cleanups and leaf removal in Grand Blanc, Grand Blanc Township and across Genesee County. We blow the leaves out, vacuum them into our leaf trailer and haul them away, then cut back the beds and blow off the drive and walks. Call [(810) 990-3040](tel:+18109903040) or [text Rob](sms:+18109903040) for a free estimate.

faq.q: Should I mulch my leaves or have them removed?
faq.a: Both have a place. MSU Extension research found lawns do fine with up to 6 inches of leaves mowed in, and the bits sift into the grass within a few weeks. When leaves come down faster than a mower can handle, or pile up deeper than 3 to 4 inches, removal is the safer call, because a thick layer under wet snow can do real damage to the grass.

faq.q: Is it bad to leave leaves on the lawn over winter?
faq.a: A thick layer, yes. MSU Extension notes that leaves piled up under wet, heavy snow can mean disaster for the grass below. A light layer chopped fine by a mower is a different story: MSU says the pieces sift into the lawn and you will not notice them in spring.

faq.q: Should I cut my grass short before winter?
faq.a: A little shorter, not short. MSU Extension suggests dropping the mower no more than one notch, typically half an inch, for the final cut, once the grass has stopped growing and the leaves are done. That keeps the lawn from going into winter too tall, which MSU says helps with snow mold and voles.

faq.q: How many leaf cleanups will my yard need?
faq.a: It depends on the trees. A yard with a few young trees may only need one visit after most of the leaves are down. A yard under big, old trees can drop more than one visit can handle. Rob will look at the trees when he comes out and tell you what makes sense.

faq.q: Do you cut back perennials in the fall?
faq.a: Yes, as much or as little as you want. Some people want every bed cleared. MSU Extension suggests leaving ornamental grasses and some perennial stems standing over winter as shelter for bees and other helpful insects, and leaves around shrubs as insulation. Tell Rob which you prefer and the beds will be done that way.

faq.q: What do you do with the leaves?
faq.a: They go in our trailer. A truck loader leaf vacuum on the front of our dump trailer pulls them in from the rows and curb piles, and we haul the load away. You are not left with a row of bags at the curb.

faq.q: How much does leaf removal cost?
faq.a: It depends on the size of the yard, how many trees drop on it and how many beds need cutting back. Rob comes out, looks at it and quotes you a price. The estimate is free.
